Title: Lung cancer.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Since tobacco smoking is the cause in vast majority of cases, the incidence of lung cancer is expected to rise in those countries with high or rising incidence of tobacco smoking. Even though populations at risk of developing lung cancer are easily identified, mass screening for lung cancer is not supported by currently available evidence. In the case of non-small cell lung cancer, a cure may be possible with surgical resection followed by post-operative chemotherapy in those diagnosed at an early stage. A small minority of patients who present with locally advanced disease may also benefit from pre-operative chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy to down stage the tumor to render it potentially operable. In a vast majority of patients, however, lung cancer presents at an advanced stage and a cure is not possible with currently available therapeutic strategies. Similarly, small cell lung cancer confined to one hemi-thorax may be curable with a combination of chemotherapy and thoracic irradiation followed by prophylactic cranial irradiation, if complete remission is achieved at the primary site. Small cell lung cancer that is spread beyond the confines of one hemi-thorax is, however, considered incurable. In this era of molecular targeted therapies, new agents are constantly undergoing pre-clinical and clinical testing with the aim of targeting the molecular pathways thought be involved in etiology and pathogenesis of lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at lung cancer, which is the top cause of death from cancer (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because most lung cancer comes from tobacco smoke, and many countries still have high or rising smoking rates (Abstract, sentence 2). You may care about this if you smoke now, smoked in the past, or care for someone with lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 2). The writers of this work review past studies to see what care helps people with different types and stages of lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 4). They also look at new drugs that aim at tiny changes in cancer cells (Abstract, sentence 9). They note that we can spot people at high risk, but wide use of lung scans for all these people is not yet backed by proof (Abstract, sentence 3). When we find non small cell lung cancer early, surgery plus drug care after surgery can sometimes cure it (Abstract, sentence 4). A few people with more local spread may gain from drug care and beam care before surgery (Abstract, sentence 5). But most people learn they have lung cancer when it is already wide spread, and cure is not now possible (Abstract, sentence 6). The paper also notes that some small cell lung cancer in one side of the chest can be cured with drug care and beam care, plus brain beam care (Abstract, sentence 7). New “target” drugs are in tests to block key cancer paths and may give more options in the future (Abstract, sentence 9).
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This research looks at lung cancer, which is the top cause of death from cancer in the world (Abstract, para. 1). It focuses on how lung cancer starts, how we find it, and how we treat it, mainly in people who smoke (Abstract, para. 1). We need this study because lung cancer cases are common and often found late, when cure is not likely (Body, para. 1). This work may help people who smoke now, people who used to smoke, and their doctors (Body, para. 2). The team reviewed large health reports and many past studies on smoking, other risks, tests, and treatments for lung cancer (Body, para. 1). They looked at how often lung cancer happens, what raises risk, and how well surgery, drugs, and radiation work (Body, para. 12). They found that smoking causes about 90% to 95% of lung cancers, and only a small share of smokers get the disease, so other body and life factors also matter (Body, para. 3). Only about 14 out of 100 people with lung cancer are alive five years after diagnosis, and cure is mainly in those found at an early stage who can have surgery and drug treatment after surgery (Body, para. 12). These findings show that stopping smoking, finding lung cancer early, and using the right mix of surgery, drugs, and radiation can help some people live longer and feel better (Body, para. 13).
